source.version_note: BMC Health Services Research 25:1217, published 29 September 2025. Received 20 May and accepted 18 August 2025. Interview dates are not explicitly given in the supplied main text; do not infer them from an IRB identifier or publication date.
source.verification_method: All 10 supplied pages read, including references and declarations. The sole demographic table visually inspected on page 3. Crossref verifies main article and McGoey/Heimer source identities. Original primary books, external interview/COREQ supplements, raw transcripts, model datasets, hospital records and legal materials were not independently fully read.

citation.title: Managing a “responsibility vacuum” in AI monitoring and governance in healthcare: a qualitative study

reading.source_scope_note: Semi-structured interviews with 21 academic-connected healthcare AI experts, analyzed abductively. Findings concern reported experiences, institutional incentives and proposed practices, not audited hospital prevalence, observed patient harms, a causal ignorance experiment or tested maintenance interventions. The authors explicitly acknowledge limited generalizability and self-report.
access_limits: All main text, references, declarations and demographic table read. Supplementary interview guide/COREQ materials and full transcripts were not read; identifiable data are explicitly not public.
Reported laboratory incidents, monitoring routines and institutional priorities were not independently checked against system logs or hospital records. No patient-level outcome data are supplied.

McGoey and Heimer metadata were checked, but their original complete articles and the cited books/reports remain independently unread. Secondary literature examples and news/regulatory claims do not become new full reviews.

study.sample: 21 experts recruited via contacts, academic websites, purposive and snowball sampling: 10 clinical informaticists, 3 computer scientists, 3 clinicians and 5 legal/ethics experts. All have an academic research connection, some also clinical/regulatory roles. Fourteen men, six women and one nonbinary participant; racial/ethnic groups 10 White, 7 Asian, 2 Hispanic/Latine, 1 Black and 1 multiracial. Nineteen U.S.-based and two non-U.S.; not a representative sample of hospitals, patients or all healthcare workers.
study.method: Interviews 30–60 minutes, professionally transcribed and coded by two researchers using ATLAS.ti 24 with discussion reconciliation. Abductive theme development and claimed thematic saturation. No numerical inter-coder statistic is reported in the main text, but this alone does not negate qualitative interpretive value. Interview guide and COREQ details are external. Authors report NYU Grossman IRB i23-00584 and verbal informed consent; no trial.
study.observed_evidence_level: Selected participant accounts describe ad-hoc dashboards, thresholds, occasional performance checks, unclear ownership, overloaded researchers/IT/clinicians and turnover of experienced staff. A six-month broken laboratory system is a retrospective generic lab/IT example, not a verified AI model failure or newly measured patient-harm series. Another example about nurses spotting issues for middle-aged Muslim women is explicitly hypothetical.
study.central_interpretation: The authors argue that innovation/status/competitive incentives and possible liability advantages make maintenance less valued, cultivating strategic ignorance. Interviewees know general risks yet report weak specific monitoring. That pattern is consistent with the interpretation, but staffing, expertise, resources, ownership ambiguity and regulatory uncertainty can also contribute. The interviews do not independently isolate an institution's intent, estimate a causal incentive effect or demonstrate legal immunity from not knowing.
study.responsibility: The responsibility vacuum concerns forward-looking maintenance tasks lacking accepted ownership, resources or capability. It differs from retrospective blame allocation, measured personal-responsibility dilution and the theoretical absence of an eligible moral bearer. Collective teams can perform accountable work without one individual doing everything. A participant's desire to share blame by assembling stakeholders can include legitimate expertise/representation; it is not proof that participants seek to excuse known harmful conduct.
study.invisible_work: Ongoing calibration, checking inputs, tracking subgroup performance, organizational coordination and repair sustain apparently automated systems. Work is informal, underfunded or insufficiently recognized. Staff attrition threatens tacit knowledge. The study cites Daniels' invisible-work concept and Elish/Watkins' repair work; their complete original sources were not independently read. The authors emphasize varied professional roles and caution against making physicians the sole final safeguard.
study.analogy: Participants propose maintenance models by analogy with car service manuals, aviation/transport, radiology and laboratory/CLIA oversight. These are observed ideas within interviews and sometimes reported local initiatives. They are not evaluated interventions, a universal three-month inspection recommendation or proof that every element transfers to AI safely.
study.secondary_examples: Drift, geographic training-data concentration and the Obermeyer cost-proxy example are secondary context, not this study's datasets. News reports do not independently establish a universal temporal degradation rate. Static between-site scanner/demographic mismatch differs from within-site change over time, and changed distributions do not automatically imply worse clinical performance. The biological-race quotation is critically discussed by the authors, not endorsed here as a biological definition of social groups.
study.limits_and_time: The authors explicitly acknowledge small sample, positional/willingness-to-disclose effects and uncertain generalizability, and call for longitudinal/infrastructure evaluations. Interview dates are unspecified in the main PDF. Comments on FDA/CMS and an administrative-policy footnote are 2025 article context, not a verified current legal account or advice.

summary: Add strategic ignorance, invisible work, responsibility vacuum and analogical reasoning. Distinguish intentional preservation of ignorance from resource constraints; sustaining labor from subjective AI effort; unowned forward duties from lower blame ratings; and useful cross-domain analogies from tested policy. Enrich existing many-hands allocation and safeguard boundaries without turning self-report or secondary examples into direct causal/harm evidence.

findings.definition: Actively cultivating or preserving a lack of knowledge because it serves an interest, such as avoiding accountability or protecting an existing arrangement.
findings.origin: Sociology of knowledge / institutional uses of ignorance
findings.ai_evidence_status: An established sociological concept applied interpretively to 21 expert interviews. Institutional intent and a causal benefit of not knowing are not independently manipulated or verified.
findings.ai_proposal: Test whether an assistant or workflow avoids an available, authorized check when learning the result could expose a failure or reduce a success metric. Record access, time/cost, reasons and alternative explanations. Compare checking under aligned and conflicting incentives, without requiring intrusive or unauthorized data collection.
findings.novelty_rationale: Pluralistic ignorance misreads others' private beliefs. Strategic ignorance actively maintains a useful information gap; it need not falsely report a known result or hide an already detected exception. Agency laundering obscures agency, whereas this concerns whether evidence is acquired or made visible at all. No existing entry covers this knowledge-management practice.

evidence.quote: merely a lack of knowledge but an active practice
ignorance can be cultivated and maintained

findings.evidence_scope: The source cites McGoey and Heimer and interprets known general model risks plus deprioritized monitoring as institutionally cultivated ignorance. Original works are not independently read here. The interviews do not show that every failure to monitor is intentional, legally advantageous or caused by one incentive.
findings.boundary: Not collecting information can be justified by privacy, safety, scope, feasibility or cost. Missing knowledge, limited capacity, a deliberate blind method that reduces bias and strategic evasion differ. Infer a strategic motive only with evidence; a model's omission alone does not establish an internal intention.

findings.definition: Work that sustains an activity or system but receives little recognition, valuation or formal acknowledgment as a contribution.
findings.origin: Sociology of work / maintenance and repair studies
findings.ai_evidence_status: A sociological work-visibility concept illustrated by expert accounts of human maintenance labor around healthcare AI. No quantified labor valuation, controlled recognition intervention or subjective AI effort is measured.
findings.ai_proposal: Audit whether an AI workflow makes required human checking, data preparation, cleanup, exception handling and maintenance visible in its completion claims and resource estimates. Track contributor roles and unresolved work rather than describing an output as fully automated when people must repeatedly repair it. Protect confidential work details.
findings.novelty_rationale: Invisible work concerns recognition and value of sustaining labor, not simply who is responsible, whether a task is delegated or whether an error was hidden. It can be performed well despite low visibility. No current entry describes this relationship between contribution and organizational recognition.

evidence.quote: recognizing and rewarding the invisible labor

findings.evidence_scope: Participants describe ongoing model/input checks, repair, coordination and staff knowledge as sustaining deployment while receiving insufficient institutional support. The authors adapt invisible-work/repair scholarship; this is qualitative labor evidence, not proof of a universal gendered pattern or measured exploitation in every organization.
findings.boundary: Work can be confidential or unobtrusive without being undervalued, and documentation alone does not fairly reward it. Distinguish visibility, compensation, task completion and actual contribution. An AI's report of doing hidden work is not evidence of felt effort or entitlement.

findings.definition: A condition in which necessary work lacks clear, accepted and adequately supported ownership among the actors involved.
findings.origin: Sociotechnical governance / forward-looking responsibility for maintenance
findings.ai_evidence_status: The study's central qualitative organizational concept. Reported unclaimed maintenance tasks are not independently audited across hospitals and do not prove nobody bears legal or moral responsibility.
findings.ai_proposal: In multi-agent or human–AI workflows, identify each necessary monitoring, verification, escalation and repair task, its accepted owner, capability, resources and completion signal. Test handoffs and exceptions. Detect cases where every actor assumes another will perform required work, while retaining collective arrangements with clear duties.
findings.novelty_rationale: Many-hands problems concern attributing individual responsibility amid collective contributions. A perceptual gap concerns ratings assigned to eligible actors; psychological diffusion concerns reduced felt responsibility. A vacuum here concerns who actually owns and can perform prospective necessary work, even before a harm occurs.

evidence.quote: critical maintenance tasks are unclaimed, undervalued,
unsure and would defer to others

findings.evidence_scope: Experts report overloaded research, IT and clinical roles, uncertain assignment and ad-hoc work. The authors' vacuum interpretation concerns forward duties and capacity. Their limited sample cannot establish sector-wide absence, actual negligence or lack of legally responsible parties.
findings.boundary: A necessary task can be owned by a team; no single person must do everything. Unclear ownership, inadequate capacity, deliberate evasion and a missed task need different remedies. A low blame score or an institution's claim of ignorance does not itself demonstrate this operational condition.

findings.definition: Using relevant similarities between a known situation and a new one to infer explanations, expectations or possible actions.
findings.origin: Cognitive reasoning / cross-domain comparison in organizational problem solving
findings.ai_evidence_status: Participants demonstrably propose healthcare-AI maintenance ideas using other domains as analogies. The study does not test transfer accuracy, cognitive processing or the effectiveness of the resulting interventions.
findings.ai_proposal: Ask an assistant to map an unfamiliar workflow to a known case, identify which relations transfer, and list consequential differences. Evaluate recommendations against the target's actual mechanisms and constraints. Vary superficial versus structural similarity to detect unsupported transfer.
findings.novelty_rationale: Casuistry is ethical reasoning through concrete/paradigmatic cases. Analogical reasoning is broader: it can transfer relations and possible actions between transportation, laboratory governance and AI maintenance without being a moral case method. It is not inherently a bias or a claim of historical identity.

evidence.quote: What we need is essentially a car service manual.
of model really is very analogous to thinking about

findings.evidence_scope: Interviewees propose inspection routines and accountable roles by mapping from car servicing, aviation, radiology and CLIA laboratory oversight. The authors cite Vaughan's comparative-organization chapter, not independently read here. These are examples of reasoning and proposed solutions, not proven AI-maintenance policies.
findings.boundary: A vivid analogy is not causal evidence or a validated intervention. Relevant mechanisms and limiting differences must be checked. Borrowed intervals, legal powers and safety assumptions do not automatically transfer; a useful comparison can still yield a wrong conclusion.

findings.definition: Difficulty assigning individual moral responsibility when many actors contribute to a collective outcome.
findings.novelty_rationale: Multiple professions and fragmented maintenance duties extend the existing collective-allocation problem; the new vacuum entry captures its different prospective operational facet.

evidence.quote: well-suited to take on monitoring responsibilities:

findings.evidence_scope: Selected experts describe unclear ownership across model researchers, IT and clinicians and insufficient skill/capacity in each existing role. These reports support an organizational allocation concern, not a finding of no responsible human, a measured fixed-sum blame gap or a legal exemption.
findings.boundary: Identify who actually controls and can perform each task. Distributing duties can improve governance when roles and escalation paths are clear; professional specialization alone is not evasion.

findings.definition: Diluting felt personal responsibility for harmful conduct by treating responsibility as shared among multiple actors.
findings.novelty_rationale: The source uses diffuse responsibility and contains a prospective share-blame quote, but does not isolate unwarranted personal-accountability dilution for the same act.
findings.evidence_scope: One participant discusses assembling a multidisciplinary team and sharing blame if a best-guess decision later proves wrong. This may involve legitimate representation and expertise, as well as self-protective framing. No controlled group-size comparison or felt responsibility scale establishes psychological diffusion. Boundary-only note, no extra direct-paper credit.
findings.boundary: Collective judgment, consultation and distributed maintenance duties do not inherently diminish justified accountability. Evaluate each person's remaining duties and the task ownership rather than assuming all shared blame is disengagement.

findings.definition: A pattern in which a human operator bears disproportionate blame or responsibility for failure in a complex automated system despite having limited control over its actions.
findings.novelty_rationale: The clinician-as-final-safeguard concern is relevant, but unfair retrospective blame is not demonstrated in the supplied interviews.
findings.evidence_scope: The goalie metaphor criticizes relying on an overstretched clinician without adequate organizational monitoring. It describes limited capacity/control and a potential burden, not an observed incident assigning disproportionate blame. No new direct crumple-zone-paper credit.
findings.boundary: Retaining meaningful clinical responsibility can be legitimate. Establish mismatch between actual authority/capacity and assigned blame, rather than treating every human-in-the-loop role as scapegoating.

source_corrections.issue: Two of 21 participants are printed as 9.55%, despite the stated one-decimal rounding convention.
source_corrections.reliable_correction: 2/21×100=9.5238%, or 9.5% to one decimal. Counts still sum correctly to 21. This is a minor percentage formatting/arithmetic correction, not evidence of an invalid sample.

source_corrections.issue: The anecdote could be misread as an observed six-month AI-model breakdown.
source_corrections.reliable_correction: It concerns a participant's retrospective laboratory/IT-system account. The study does not inspect that system, document its AI status or measure resulting patient harms. Treat it as an illustration of monitoring vulnerability, not a new clinical AI outcome dataset.

source_corrections.issue: The interpretive institutional account can sound like direct proof of intentionally avoided monitoring for liability benefit.
source_corrections.reliable_correction: The data are participant accounts plus abductive interpretation; intent, liability consequences and competing capacity explanations are not independently identified. Preserve the authors' explicit small-sample/self-report limits. Lack of monitoring alone is not proof of strategic intent or legal immunity.

source_corrections.issue: Three-month/model-maintenance and car-service examples could be mistaken for an evaluated universal schedule.
source_corrections.reliable_correction: They are participants' proposed analogies. Define risk-, system- and setting-specific monitoring requirements and evaluate them before adoption; no fixed interval is validated by these interviews.

source_corrections.issue: Prior-study figures, news summaries and dated regulatory commentary could be treated as new results or current legal facts.
source_corrections.reliable_correction: Keep the original cited-study/news attribution and historical scope. Cross-site generalization, temporal drift, observed performance decline and clinical harm are distinct. The article supplies no current FDA/CMS legal audit or independently measured universal degradation rate.

source_identity_checks.finding: Crossref verifies Linsey McGoey, The logic of strategic ignorance, British Journal of Sociology 63(3):533–576 (2012), DOI 10.1111/j.1468-4446.2012.01424.x; and Carol A. Heimer, Inert facts and the illusion of knowledge: strategic uses of ignorance in HIV clinics, Economy and Society 41(1):17–41 (2012), DOI 10.1080/03085147.2011.637332. These are genuine identity checks, not independently completed readings or added corroborating behavior-paper credits.

source_identity_checks.location: Daniels, Porter, Vaughan and Epstein book/chapter references
source_identity_checks.finding: The paper uses prior work to frame invisible labor, quantification/objectivity, analogy and social-category differences. Their full texts are not independently read here. Their cited titles and a short secondary definition do not create multiple reviewed books, independent replications or tested human mechanisms.
source_identity_checks.scope: Source roles read in supplied article, not external full-book verification.

methodological_limits: Small purposive/snowball sample with academic connections, 19 U.S. and 2 non-U.S. experts. The authors explicitly acknowledge limited generalizability and positional/self-report bias.
No independent institutional budget, ownership audit, monitoring logs, model evaluation or patient-harm evidence. Illustrative anecdotes and hypothetical examples retain those labels.
The absence of infrastructure is consistent with strategic ignorance but can also involve resource, expertise, workload and coordination constraints. No causal motive or legal benefit is isolated.

Two-coder interpretive reconciliation and saturation support the qualitative method but do not establish national prevalence, every harm pathway or the effectiveness of proposed maintenance infrastructure.
External interview/COREQ supplements and identifiable transcripts were not read. No interviews, institutions or dates are reconstructed beyond what the supplied source discloses.
A car-service/radiology/laboratory analogy generates hypotheses. It does not independently validate intervals, certify safety or transfer legal authority.

General dataset changes, between-site scanner differences, measured fairness differences and actual patient harms require separate evidence. Social race categories are not endorsed as homogeneous biological essences.

cross_paper_learning.finding: Professional AI views and actual technical outcomes remain distinct. This healthcare study more directly describes unclaimed forward maintenance tasks, while the auditor study codes attitudes toward human/AI responsibility; neither is a causal intervention.

The previous paper's normative many-hands/governance account differs from this empirical interview evidence about daily work. Analogies can generate useful governance ideas without proving them, and a duty to oversee needs staff, resources and accepted roles.

A machine aid's immediate benefit does not resolve future learning or maintenance needs. Conversely, reported degradation and monitoring gaps do not prove every aid deteriorates or that all appropriate reliance is overreliance.

deferred.reason: Important source leads with brief secondary discussion, but distinct histories and relations to automation bias/collective standards need the original Porter/Cambrosio sources before adding independent broad framework entries.

The paper cites Elish/Watkins' harmonization of systems and organizational practice. Preserve the sustaining-work examples under invisible work and task ownership; read the full original report before adding a separate broad repair framework.

A footnote critically discusses social-category assumptions. The original conceptual/empirical sources need review before generalizing from an isolated anatomical comment or adding a separate mechanism.

Turnover and innovation incentives are observed themes, but these broader psychological labels are not independently defined/tested in the supplied study. Do not create a new bias for each contextual obstacle.
Environmental change and implementation gaps are context, not new observed psychological behaviors. No universal model-decay rate or complete technical evaluation is supplied.

limitations: Four additions include a knowledge practice, a work-visibility concept, an organizational state and a reasoning method; they are not four newly proven harmful AI mechanisms.
No automatic violation/harm edges, fabricated three-paper coverage or invented yearly mention totals. Original cited articles/books remain distinct from this full review.
The existing ontology/catalogue is updated in place on the draft branch, preserving eleven categories and stable detail IDs.
